list-item.p: Lenalidomide 20 mg can safely be added to RAdR for patients with R/R TCL.
RAdR shows activity in R/R TCL and may effectively bridge to consolidation.

abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: Targeted therapies can induce responses in patients with relapsed/refractory T-cell lymphoma (R/R TCL) but are not curative. Genetic mutations associated with epigenetic and transcriptional dysregulation are common in many TCL subtypes, and drugs that modulate the epigenome and that target transcriptional regulators have synergistic activity in TCL. We hypothesized that fixed duration treatment with multiagent combinations of these drugs could produce deep responses leading to durable remissions. In a phase 1 trial, we tested escalating doses of lenalidomide added to romidepsin, azacitidine, and dexamethasone (RAdR) for patients with R/R TCL. The primary objective was to identify the maximum tolerated dose (MTD) of lenalidomide that could safely be used in RAdR. Secondary end points included response rate, survival, and markers of immune activation. Twenty-six patients enrolled and 21 were evaluable for response. Adverse events were predominantly gastrointestinal and hematologic. Grade 3/4 thrombocytopenia and neutropenia occurred in 19% and 21% of cycles, respectively. The MTD of lenalidomide was 20 mg. Among 9 patients treated at the MTD the objective response rate was 89% and complete response rate 22%. At 1 year, the estimated rate of progression-free survival was 14% and overall survival was 66%. Cell line models of anaplastic large cell lymphoma were interrogated to explore the activity of drug combinations in responding genetic subtypes. RAdR demonstrated activity in patients with highly refractory TCL but did not induce durable responses. This novel combination effectively bridged some patients with refractory TCL to consolidation such as allogeneic transplantation. This trial was registered at www.ClinicalTrials.gov as NCT04447027.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: T-cell lymphomas (TCL) are a heterogeneous group of mature T-cell malignancies with overlapping biological features.1,2 Mutations in epigenetic regulators such as TET2, DNMT3A, and IDH2 are observed in 20% to 80% of peripheral TCL (PTCL), with higher rates in angioimmunoblastic TCL (AITL) and follicular helper T-cell subtypes of PTCL.3, 4, 5 Dysregulated transcription is also a common feature of TCL including overexpression of IRF4, which regulates transcription factors involved in lymphocyte growth and differentiation.6 Finally, stromal cell driven differential gene expression signatures in TCL samples have been correlated with distinct TCL subtypes and clinical outcomes, suggesting that alterations of the tumor environment are driven by TCL biology and may provide an opportunity for therapeutic intervention.7, 8, 9, 10

Drugs that target the epigenetic regulatory program, including the histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibitor romidepsin, and the hypomethylating agent azacitidine, are active in TCL cell line models.11, 12, 13 Lenalidomide degrades IRF4 and other key transcription factors such as IKZF1 and IKZF3, which are key vulnerabilities in TCL cell lines,14, 15, 16 and lowers the threshold for natural killer (NK) cell activation promoting antitumor immune response.17,18 Cell line and ex vivo models of TCL identified synergistic induction of apoptosis when romidepsin was combined with either azacitidine or lenalidomide, suggesting these combinations could be potent therapeutic options for patients with TCL.19, 20, 21

Clinically, TCL frequently exhibit resistance to conventional therapies,22, 23, 24, 25 the median survival for patients with relapsed or refractory (R/R) PTCL treated with salvage chemotherapy is ∼6 months without stem cell transplant consolidation.26 Targeted agents, which are administered as indefinite therapy are active in R/R PTCL but do not significantly change the natural history as the median progression-free survival (PFS) with these drugs is ∼3 to 6 months, and allogeneic stem cell transplantation remains the only potentially curative treatment for most patients with R/R PTCL.27, 28, 29, 30 Single-agent response rates with romidepsin are ∼30% in PTCL and cutaneous TCL and the response rate to azacitidine in AITL/follicular helper T-cell subtypes of PTCL is 33%.31, 32, 33, 34 Lenalidomide has a single-agent response rate of 22% in R/R PTCL and 42% in adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma (ATLL).35,36

Phase 2 trials, which tested doublets of romidepsin with azacitidine, or romidepsin with lenalidomide showed response rates of ∼60%.37,38 Increased drug toxicity is observed with combination therapy, which is a limitation of these regimens, especially when delivered over an extended treatment duration. Although response rates are higher with targeted therapy doublets, most patients eventually develop tumors that are resistant to therapy. It is unknown whether time-limited, multiagent synergistic drug combinations can induce deeper and more durable responses in patients with R/R PTCL, thus obviating the need for allogeneic stem cell transplantation or extended duration of therapy.

We hypothesized that treatment with romidepsin, azacitidine, lenalidomide, and dexamethasone (RAdR), by simultaneously blocking multiple critical survival pathways and inducing antitumor immune activation, would lead to durable remissions with time-limited, cyclic administration of drugs. Here, we present the results of a phase 1 clinical trial.

sec.title: Eligibility criteria
sec.p: Eligible patients were aged ≥18 years with a mature TCL, confirmed by the laboratory of pathology at the National Cancer Institute,1,2 which had relapsed after, or progressed during, at least 1 line of previous systemic therapy. Patients with anaplastic large cell lymphoma (ALCL) or CD30+ mycosis fungoides (MF) or Sézary syndrome were required to have received previous brentuximab vedotin. Previous autologous or allogeneic stem cell transplantation was allowed. Patients needed to have at least 1 measurable lesion by International Working Group Consensus Response Evaluation Criteria in Lymphoma (RECIL 2017)39 or modified severity-weighted assessment tool (mSWAT)40 criteria or to have an abnormal clonal T-cell population detectable by peripheral blood flow cytometry; an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status score of ≤2, or ≤3 if the decreased performance status was deemed to be due to disease; and adequate organ function manifested by an absolute neutrophil count cutoff to 1 X 103/μL and platelets to 75 X 103/μL, total bilirubin of ≤1.5 times the institutional upper limit of normal, and serum creatinine of ≤1.5 mg/dL. Treatment with 1 previous study drug was allowed. Patients with a history of inflammatory bowel disease or other malabsorptive conditions that could impede oral drug delivery were excluded. Additionally, patients with clinically significant cardiovascular disease and those with baseline QTC prolongation were excluded. Pregnant and lactating women were not eligible due to the know teratogenic effects of lenalidomide. Full study eligibility criteria are listed in the supplemental Methods.

sec.title: Study design and treatment schedule
sec.p: We conducted a single-center, open label, phase 1 trial of RAdR in R/R TCL. A “3+3” design was used to identify the maximum tolerated dose (MTD) of dose-escalated lenalidomide with fixed dose romidepsin, azacitidine, and dexamethasone. An expansion cohort of 9 patients was treated at the MTD. Patients first received a 7-day course of oral lenalidomide for correlative research followed by up to 6 21-day cycles of IV romidepsin (12 mg/m2; days 1 and 10), oral azacitidine (300 mg; days 1-10), oral dexamethasone (40 mg; days 1 and 10), and oral lenalidomide (5 mg to 20 mg; days 1-10). Four dose levels of lenalidomide were evaluated, 5 mg, 10 mg, 15 mg, and 20 mg. After completing the dose-escalation phase of the study, the protocol was amended to remove the lenalidomide lead-in and to extend the cycle length to 28 days (supplemental Methods). The dose modification strategy is described in the supplemental Methods. The approach for hematologic toxicity was to first hold azacitidine and lenalidomide for grade ≥3 toxicity and dose reduced in subsequent cycles. Romidepsin was dose reduced in the setting of recurrent grade 3/4 hematologic toxicity. There was no maintenance therapy after the planned 6 cycles and allogeneic stem cell transplant consolidation was allowed. Patients not on anticoagulation received 81 mg aspirin daily for venous thromboembolism prophylaxis. All patients received growth factor support and prophylaxis against Pneumocystis jirovecii. Patients with active central nervous system lymphoma received intrathecal methotrexate and/or cytarabine in addition to RAdR.

The study was approved by the institutional review board of the National Cancer Institute and was supported by the Intramural Research Program of the National Institutes of Health. The trial was registered at www.ClinicalTrials.gov (identifier: NCT04447027). This study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.

sec.title: Outcomes
sec.p: The primary end point of the study was to determine the MTD of lenalidomide and overall safety of the RAdR regimen. Safety assessments included the frequency of treatment-emergent adverse events (AE) grouped by severity of the AE as defined by the Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events, version 5. Safety was assessed in all patients. The dose-limiting toxicity (DLT) window was from day 1 of cycle 1 until day 1 of cycle 2, before initiation of cycle 2 treatment. Events in the DLT window were used to determine the MTD using the 3+3 method (supplemental Methods). Secondary end points included the overall response rate (ORR), complete response rate (CR), duration of response (DOR), PFS, and overall survival (OS). Response was assessed using RECIL 2017 in patients with PTCL along with mSWAT in patients with cutaneous TCL, and the consensus criteria in patients with ATLL who had leukemic disease.41 Computed tomography scans were obtained at baseline and after cycles 2, 4, and 6, and positron emission tomography scans were performed at baseline and after cycle 6. mSWAT measurements were performed in collaboration with the department of dermatology after cycle 2, 4, and 6. Patients in remission after completing the planned 6 cycles of treatment were followed up every 60 days for the first 6 months, every 90 days from 6 to 30 months, every 6 months from 30 to 54 months, and annually thereafter.

Whole-exome sequencing was performed in a subset of patients as part of the routine diagnostic evaluation of biopsy samples by the laboratory of pathology at the National Cancer Institute. Circulating B-cell, T-cell, and NK cell numbers were assessed before each cycle of therapy by peripheral blood flow cytometry.

sec.title: Cell line and correlative studies
sec.p: The relative viability of the following ALCL cell line models, KIJK (anaplastic lymphoma kinase [ALK]–positive ALCL), DL40 (TP63-rearranged ALK-negative ALCL), FE-PD (DUSP22-rearranged ALK-negative ALCL) and MAC2A (triple-negative ALCL), was assessed by luminescence after treatment with RAdR (supplemental Methods).

sec.title: Statistical considerations
sec.p: Descriptive statistics including mean, standard deviation, median, and range for continuous variables such as age, frequency counts, and percentages for categorical variables such as stage and response status are provided with differences assessed using the t test. The best response rates and their 95% confidence intervals (CI) using the exact method are reported. The Kaplan-Meier method was used to estimate OS, PFS, and DOR, with patients censored at time of allogeneic stem cell transplantation. All survival outcomes were assessed from time of study enrollment. OS was defined as time to death; PFS as time to progression date or death whichever came first; DOR was defined as time from earliest response to progression date or death whichever came first. The data cutoff date was 1 January 2025.

sec.title: Patient characteristics
sec.p: A total of 37 patients were screened and 26 patients with R/R TCL were enrolled between December 2020 and November 2023 (supplemental Figure 1). Patients had received a median of 2 previous lines of therapy (range, 1-8) including 8 (31%) who had received ≥4 previous lines of therapy and 2 (8%) patients who had received previous allogeneic stem cell transplantation. Fifteen patients (58%) had a nodal PTCL, 8 with PTCL not otherwise specified (PTCL, NOS; 31%), 5 (19%) with AITL, and 2 (8%) with ALK-negative ALCL, both DUSP22-rearranged. Patients with nonnodal TCL subtypes accounted for 38%, including 6 (23%) patients with MF and 4 (15%) with ATLL, 3 acute and 1 lymphomatous. Median mSWAT at baseline in patients with MF was 18.7 (range, 6.3-52.6). Baseline characteristics, including in those treated at the MTD (n = 9), are summarized in Table 1.

sec.title: Safety
sec.p: Among 26 patients enrolled in the study, 2 DLTs were observed, grade 4 thrombocytopenia at dose level 1 (lenalidomide 5 mg) and grade 3 abdominal pain at dose level 2 (lenalidomide 10 mg). The MTD of lenalidomide was determined to be 20 mg. Most treatment-emergent AE were grade 1 to 2. Hematologic and gastrointestinal toxicity was the most common (Figure 1; supplemental Table 1). The most frequent grade 3/4 nonhematologic AE were hypokalemia (11%), kidney injury (8%), adrenal insufficiency (8%), fatigue (8%), anorexia (8%), weight loss (8%), and infection (8%). Hematologic AE that were grade 3/4 were observed in 35% of cycles and included neutropenia (21%), thrombocytopenia (19%), and anemia (14%). Grade 3/4 neutropenia and thrombocytopenia occurred in 46% and 35% of patients, respectively. There were no opportunistic infections or treatment-related deaths. To date, all deaths have been due to disease progression.

sec.p: Seven (29%) patients required dose reduction, most frequently due to thrombocytopenia. Dose reductions (percentage of cycles) occurred in lenalidomide (15%), azacitidine (9%), and romidepsin (2%). Twenty-nine (33%) of all cycles were delayed due to cytopenia. Because of the frequent need for dose delays, the study schedule was amended to increase the cycle length from 21 to 28 days after completing the dose-escalation phase and determining the MTD. To mitigate delays in treatment, the lenalidomide lead-in was also removed in the expansion cohort.

sec.title: Efficacy of RAdR in R/R TCL
sec.p: Of 26 patients enrolled in the study, 2 discontinued during the lenalidomide lead-in and were not included in the efficacy analyses. Both withdrew from the study for alternative therapies. Among 24 patient who received at least 1 cycle of RAdR, the median number of cycles were 4 (range, 1-6); 8 (33%) patients completed the planned 6 cycles of RAdR. In total, 10 (42%) discontinued for progression, and 6 (25%) patients stopped therapy before the planned 6 cycles due to toxicity, 4 due to thrombocytopenia, 1 abdominal pain, and 1 due to anxiety.

Three patients discontinued treatment before the first response assessment (supplemental Figure 1). Among evaluable patients (n = 21) 3 had a CR (14%; 2 ALK-negative ALCL and 1 PTCL, NOS), 11 (52%) achieved partial response (PR), 2 (10%) had stable disease, and 5 (24%) had progressive disease (Figure 2A). Eight patients (89%) treated at the MTD had a response, including 2 (22%) who achieved CR, 6 (67%) who achieved PR, and 1 (11%) who had stable disease (Figure 2B). In patients with nodal PTCL (n = 15), 3 (20%) had a CR and 7 (47%) achieved PR (supplemental Figure 2).

sec.p: After a median follow-up of 20.4 months, the median PFS was 3.9 months (95% CI, 2.4-9.4), and the median OS was not reached (95% CI, 7.4 months to not reached; Figure 3A-B). The estimated rate of PFS at 1-year was 14% (95% CI, 5-40) and OS was 66% (95% CI, 50-88). Among patients treated at the MTD, 1-year PFS was 11% (95% CI, 2-71) and OS was 78% (95% CI, 55-100; Figure 3C-D). Estimated PFS and OS in nodal PTCL at 1 year was 16% (95% CI, 5-55) and 73% (95% CI, 54-100), respectively (supplemental Figure 3). The median DOR in all patients was 4.3 months (interquartile range, 2.1-9.6). Six patients (25%) received allogeneic stem cell transplantation, including 3 of 9 patients treated at the MTD, all of whom remain alive at last follow-up. Survival by subtype is shown in supplemental Figure 4.

sec.title: Exceptional responders
sec.p: Two patients had remissions lasting ≥3 years after completing 6 cycles of RAdR without consolidation. The first patient had a history of lymphocytic-variant hypereosinophilic syndrome with subsequent diagnosis of PTCL, NOS consistent with the GATA3 subtype (GATA3 and CCR4 positive by immunohistochemistry).42 He had a CR with RAdR and declined allogeneic stem cell transplant consolidation. Despite having been refractory to his 3 previous lines of therapy, he remained in remission for 42 months off treatment before disease relapse. Whole-exome sequencing in this patient revealed a nonsense mutation in PRDM1 (c.1677C>G; variant allele frequency, 44%) and no other pathogenic alterations. The second patient, with MF, had received 4 previous lines of therapy including CHOP (cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, Oncovin [vincristine], and prednisone) chemotherapy, brentuximab vedotin, mogamulizumab, and a checkpoint inhibitor. He had a PR to RAdR with residual positron emission tomography avidity in his lower extremities but has not experienced disease progression for 36 months after completing RAdR. Both patients with ALK-negative ALCL had a CR with durations of 3 and 13 months, respectively.

sec.title: Biomarkers of response to RAdR
sec.p: Baseline levels of circulating NK cell were similar in responders (n = 10) and nonresponders (n = 5) but significantly increased with subsequent cycles in patients who had a clinical response to RAdR (Figure 4A). Mean NK cells per microliter were 90.5 before cycle 1 and 143.9 before cycle 2 (P = .039) in responders. The highest levels were observed before cycle 5 (mean, 195 NK cells per μL). In contrast, circulating NK cells numerically decreased in nonresponders, 88 NK cells per μL before cycle 1 and 67.5 cells per μL before cycle 2 (P = .22). No increase in NK cells was observed after the lenalidomide lead-in (cycle 0-1) among RAdR responders or nonresponders. In patients who completed the planned 6 cycles of RAdR, levels of circulating NK cells remained above pretreatment levels until initiation of the next line of therapy or allogeneic transplantation (Figure 4B). Circulating levels of CD3+/CD4+, CD3+/CD8+, and CD19+ cells, excluding patients with significant circulating lymphoma cells, were numerically lower in nonresponders at baseline but did not significantly change with subsequent cycles of RAdR (supplemental Figure 5).

sec.title: RAdR in ALCL cell lines
sec.p: Noting the unexpected clinical activity with RAdR in patients with ALCL, we further investigated this observation using representative cell line models of this disease. The addition of subinhibitory concentrations of romidepsin to low-dose azacitidine and lenalidomide led to significant ALCL cell line death in MAC2A cells (triple-negative ALCL) at low and intermediate doses of romidepsin and in FE-PD cells (DUSP22-rearranged ALCL) at intermediate romidepsin dosing (supplemental Figures 5 and 6). In MAC2A cells the combination of romidepsin, azacitidine, and lenalidomide, at concentrations that did not induce significant cell killing as doublets, (ie, azacitidine and romidepsin, azacitidine and lenalidomide, or romidepsin and lenalidomide) led to a 65% reduction in viable tumor cells (P = .003; Figure 5A). Similarly, in FE-PD cells, there was a 61% increase in tumor cell killing (P < .0001), which was approximately twice that observed with doublets (Figure 5B). In DL40 cells (TP63-rearranged ALCL) and KIJK cells (ALK-positive ALCL) the combination of lenalidomide and azacitidine significantly increased cell line killing, but the addition of romidepsin did not increase cell killing (Figure 5C-D; supplemental Figures 6 and 7). There was no appreciable dose response to single-agent dexamethasone in the tested cell lines; therefore, dexamethasone was not included in combination with the other components of RAdR in cell line experiments (supplemental Figure 8).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: We showed that lenalidomide 20 mg can safely be used in the multitargeted RAdR regimen to induce responses in patients with R/R TCL and served as a bridge to consolidation. Patients with chemotherapy-refractory TCL have limited treatment options given the high frequency of resistant tumors and baseline cytopenia. Grade 3/4 thrombocytopenia was a particularly challenging toxicity with RAdR, especially in older patients and heavily pretreated patients. Previous studies with these drugs as single agents reported a similar safety profile, with grade 3/4 thrombocytopenia in ∼20% and neutropenia in 20% to 40% of patients.32,33,35 Studies of romidepsin with either azacitidine or lenalidomide in PTCL have found grade 3/4 thrombocytopenia and neutropenia in 34% to 48% of patients.37,38 Rates of grade 3/4 thrombocytopenia and neutropenia with RAdR were observed in 35% and 46% of patients, respectively. Despite the potential for significant toxicity by combining these agents, the MTD was established as the highest dose of lenalidomide tested. Extending the treatment cycle length from 21 to 28 days allowed for more effective dosing, as evidenced by the fact that only 2 of 9 patients treated at the MTD (28-day cycle) discontinued due to toxicity. This study did not directly compare the toxicity profile of RAdR with that of previous studies using targeted therapy doublets, but we acknowledge that the addition of lenalidomide to romidepsin and azacitidine has the potential to increase toxicity and cause treatment delays, particularly due to cytopenias.

Previous studies of single-agent romidepsin, azacitidine, and lenalidomide have reported an ORR and CR in patients with R/R TCL of ∼30% and ∼15%, respectively, and a median PFS of ∼4 months.31, 32, 33, 34, 35,43 In a phase 2 trial of romidepsin and azacitidine in untreated or R/R PTCL, the ORR was 61% and CR 48%, with a median PFS of 8 months.37 A phase 2 trial of romidepsin and lenalidomide conducted in older or unfit patients with untreated PTCL found an ORR of 65% and CR of 26%.38 In our study of RAdR, the ORR was 58%, and 89% in patients treated at the MTD, most of whom were treated on a 28-day cycle. The rate of CR was 14% in all patients and 22% at the MTD. Despite leading to a response in most patients, only 33% completed the planned 6 cycles due to early disease progression and toxicity.

Although previous studies have shown higher response rates with these agents in AITL, only 2 (50%) evaluable patients with AITL treated with RAdR had a response, both of which were PR. There were no patients with AITL treated at the MTD. Although crosstrial comparisons should be interpreted with caution, it is possible that the lower-than-expected activity of RAdR in patients with AITL was due to the relatively lower doses of romidepsin and azacitidine used with RAdR compared with romidepsin and azacitidine doublets. Interestingly, both patients with ALK-negative ALCL in this study had a CR, although neither was durable. This was unexpected because previous clinical trials with HDAC inhibitors have reported numerically lower response rates in ALCL compared with other PTCL subtypes.31,44 Increased DNA hypomethylation is observed in the clinically favorable DUSP22-rearranged subtype of ALCL and therefore hypomethylating drugs such as azacitidine may induce the molecular profile of this clinically favorable subtype.45 To further explore this we evaluated the activity of RAdR in ALCL cell lines. Compared with 2 drug combinations of romidepsin, azacitidine, and lenalidomide, the triplet induced significant tumor cell killing in triple-negative (MAC2A) and DUSP22-rearranged (FE-PD) ALK-negative ALCL lines. If confirmed in larger cohorts of patients with ALCL, these observations could suggest that the RAdR regimen would be active in DUSP22-rearranged and triple-negative ALCL subtypes, which make up >90% of ALK-negative ALCL.46

Two patients had durable remissions lasting >3 years without consolidation; 1 was a patient with GATA3 PTCL, NOS whose tumor had a PRDM1 nonsense mutation. These mutations are more commonly observed in ALCL in which it has been shown to lead to the constitutive overexpression of IRF4.47 IRF4, BATF3, and IKZF1 form a critical transcriptional regulatory unit in ALCL leading to activation of MYC, among other targets.47,48 Interestingly, the 3 CRs that were observed in this study occurred in 2 patients with ALK-negative ALCL and the aforementioned patient with PTCL, NOS, suggesting that dependence on this transcriptional program may be a biomarker of response to RAdR. Given the small number of patients in this study, this observation should be further evaluated in independent cohorts. Consistent with this hypothesis, the ALK-negative cell lines MAC2A and FE-PD, which are known to rely upon the superenhancers IRF4, BATF3, and IKZF1,48 demonstrated increased sensitivity to treatment with the combination of romidepsin, azacitidine, and lenalidomide.

In addition to targeting IRF4, lenalidomide has immunomodulatory properties including NK cell activation.17 We evaluated circulating NK cell levels before each cycle of RAdR and found a significant and progressive increase in responders but not in nonresponders to RAdR. Although we note this association, we are unable to determine in this study whether the relationship is causal. NK cells did not increase during the single-agent lenalidomide lead-in, suggesting that either a longer period of treatment or combination with other agents was required to increase NK cell levels. Previous studies have shown that treatment with hypomethylating agents, such as azacitidine, upregulate immune-related genes and increase sensitivity of primary tumor cells to NK cell–mediated killing.49 HDAC inhibitors also increase NK cell activation and tumor cell killing by NK cells.50 We hypothesize that RAdR may synergistically increase NK cell activation, enhancing antitumor immunity. Bispecific NK cell–engaging antibodies are currently in clinical development for the treatment of TCL and these results suggest that RAdR, or a RAdR-like regimen, could be successfully combined with these therapies.51 Previous studies by our group have shown that the antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity of monoclonal antibodies can be enhanced by activating NK cells,52, 53, 54 and the results of our study also suggest that the clinical activity of RAdR could be improved by combining it with monoclonal antibodies directed at TCL antigens. The results of this study do not allow us to definitively determine whether RAdR directly or indirectly increases NK cells; but, in contrast to chemotherapy, it does not decrease NK cell levels and would therefore be a rational treatment to combine with NK cell–engaging therapies regardless of the precise mechanism. Retrospective analyses of NK cell activation from previous studies of targeted therapies in TCL are encouraged and may help validate the findings from this trial.

The acceptable safety profile and high response rates observed with RAdR, particularly at the MTD, are a proof of principle that 4 drug targeted therapy regimens can be safely used to treat patients with TCL. Despite the high response rate with RAdR, the median DOR was short, at ∼4 months. Although there were rare durable remissions, most patients on study who did not receive allogeneic stem cell transplant consolidation experienced disease relapsed. These results highlight the need for more robust preclinical models and more effective targeted therapies to optimize the development of synergistic combination regimens for R/R TCL.

The small and heterogenous cohort of patients treated on this study limit our ability to accurately estimate the activity or safety of RAdR in specific TCL subtypes and limits our ability to indirectly compare results with previous studies of combination targeted therapy in TCL. This also limits our ability to identify robust biomarkers of response. Similar limitations apply to the patients treated at the MTD in this study.

This trial tested the hypothesis that synergistic combinations of targeted therapies would be curative in patients with R/R TCL. Although RAdR did not achieve this goal, we note that responses were seen across TCL subtypes and were particularly high in patients with nodal PTCL and in those treated at the MTD. RAdR was an effective means of bridging patients to allogeneic transplantation, which is currently the only curative treatment for most patients with R/R TCL, and RAdR may be considered as a therapeutic option for these patients.
